nodes.label: Paskevich and early governors
nodes.full: Ivan Paskevich (1827–1831) and his successors Baron Rosen (1831–1837), Golovin and Neidhardt governed the Caucasus as commanders of a separate Caucasus Corps, with military governors of the new provinces and the Georgian, Armenian and Muslim elites incorporated into the imperial nobility. The administration was military, centralised and arbitrary.
nodes.src: Ronald Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994); Moshe Gammer, Muslim Resistance to the Tsar (1994).

nodes.label: Vorontsov
nodes.full: Prince Mikhail Vorontsov, the first Viceroy of the Caucasus from 1844, a liberal-minded aristocrat who had governed New Russia, won Georgian and Armenian nobles by respect for their rank, opened schools, a theatre and newspapers, encouraged trade and cities, and put Tbilisi on the cultural map; his rule is remembered as a good time for the region.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Firuz Kazemzadeh, Russia and the Caucasus (in Pipes); Gammer 1994.

nodes.label: Baryatinsky and Grand Duke Mikhail
nodes.full: Prince Alexander Baryatinsky (1856–1862), who completed the conquest of the North Caucasus, and Grand Duke Mikhail Nikolaevich (Viceroy 1862–1881), who introduced the Great Reforms to Transcaucasia, led an administration which enlisted the nobility and townspeople and which, with the dismantling of the khanates, put the Caucasus on a Russian provincial footing.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Audrey Altstadt, The Azerbaijani Turks (1992).

nodes.label: Georgian nobles in service
nodes.full: The Georgian nobility, with some 5 per cent of the population, was admitted to the Russian nobility in 1830s lists with its titles of prince (knyaz) and noble (aznauri), keeping its estates and serfs, and its sons served as officers and officials, with a few, such as Grigol Orbeliani, rising to the highest rank; at the same time the old kingdom's elite lost its political role.

nodes.label: Muslim beks
nodes.full: The families of the former khans and the beks of Azerbaijan were recognised as nobles in 1840s and 1850s, kept their lands and their legal privileges, and supplied officers and officials to the Russian administration; some became generals and writers, and the tsarist state used them as its local partners among the Muslims.

nodes.label: Armenian merchant families
nodes.full: The Armenian meliks' families, enrolled as nobles in Russia, and the rich Armenian merchant houses of Tbilisi were by the 1860s the main commercial class of the city and the largest group in its municipal electorate, giving Armenians a leading role in its commerce and municipal government.
nodes.src: Suny 1994; Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993).

nodes.label: Conspiracy of 1832
nodes.full: A group of young Georgian nobles, Prince Okropir (Okropir) Bagration, Solomon Dodashvili, Alexander Orbeliani and others, plotted in 1830–1832 to restore the monarchy with the tsarevich, opposed the new Russian administration and sought to rise in Tbilisi; the plot was betrayed in December 1832, and the conspirators exiled to Siberia and Russia. It became the Georgian national legend of resistance.
nodes.src: Court of inquiry records; Suny 1994; Rapp 2003.

nodes.label: Shamil at Tsinandali
nodes.full: In July 1854 the imam Shamil's cavalry from Dagestan, in the Caucasian War, rode into Kakheti and captured the estate of Tsinandali, taking two princesses, Anna Chavchavadze and Varvara Orbeliani, and their families as hostages; they were held for eight months and then exchanged for Shamil's son Jamal al-Din in 1855. The raid was the last great action on Georgian soil.
nodes.src: Anna Chavchavadze's recollections; Gammer 1994; Lesley Blanch, The Sabres of Paradise (1960).

nodes.label: Crimean War: Kars
nodes.full: In the Crimean War the Russian Caucasus army under Bebutov defeated the Ottomans at Bashgedikler in 1853, and after Muravyov's siege General Williams surrendered the fortress of Kars on 28 November 1855 to Muravyov-Karsky; the capture strengthened Russia's bargaining position, but Kars was returned at the peace of Paris in 1856.

nodes.label: War of 1877–1878
nodes.full: In 1877 two Russian columns took Ardahan in May and, after setbacks at Zivin, Kars on 18 November, helped by Armenian and Georgian officers, among them Loris-Melikov; the eastern front pinned the Ottoman field armies. Batum was handed over after the armistice in 1878; the Berlin settlement confirmed Russia's possession of Kars, Ardahan and Batum.
nodes.src: Treaty of Berlin (13 July 1878), arts. 58–60; William Allen and Paul Muratoff, Caucasian Battlefields (1953).

nodes.label: Abkhaz rising
nodes.full: In 1866 the Abkhaz of Sukhum district, resentful at the abolition of their princedom in 1864, at Russian rule and at Orthodox conversion, rose at Lykhny and killed Russian officers; the revolt was put down with force and its aftermath saw the exile of large numbers of Abkhaz to the Ottoman empire. Abkhaz and Georgian accounts of the cause and of the exile differ.
nodes.src: Imperial reports; Stephen Jones in Cambridge History; Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Risings in Guria and Imereti
nodes.full: Peasants of Guria rose in 1841 against the imposition of Russian taxes and conscription, as did Imereti in 1857 when the nobles' labour dues were being revised and abolished, and a number of these risings were put down with troops; they were a sign of the rural discontent which the later emancipation tried to meet.

nodes.label: Provinces of 1846
nodes.full: In 1846 the government divided the Caucasus into the provinces of Tbilisi and Kutaisi (Georgia and Imereti), Shemakha (from 1859, Baku), Derbent and the Black Sea district, with the Armenian oblast later turned into the Erivan province in 1849; later the Elisavetpol province was made in 1868. The structure remained until 1917.

nodes.label: Emancipation
nodes.full: The Russian emancipation law of 1861 was applied in the Caucasus on the nobility's terms in successive decrees from 1864 to 1871, beginning with the province of Tbilisi and then Imereti, Guria, Mingrelia and Abkhazia, and from 1870 for Armenian and Muslim peasants; the serfs gained personal freedom but had to pay redemption for land and the nobles kept much of the best of it, so much discontent remained.

nodes.label: Muslim spiritual boards
nodes.full: Under the statute of 1872 the Russian government created two Transcaucasian Muslim Spiritual Boards, one for Shias at Tbilisi under a sheikh-ul-Islam and one for the Sunnis under a mufti, to regulate the mosques, clergy and personal law of the Muslims and thereby to incorporate them into the imperial system.

nodes.label: Georgian exarchate
nodes.full: Under the Russian exarchs the Georgian church was kept in subordination to the Holy Synod, with Russian bishops on the Georgian sees and the Georgian liturgy replaced by Church Slavonic in many parishes, and the use of the Georgian language in schools and church was restricted, a policy that was a main grievance of Georgian national movement.

nodes.label: Armenian Statute
nodes.full: The Statute (Polozhenie) of 1836 defined the Catholicos as head of the Armenian Church in Russia, with an elected synod under the oversight of a Russian procurator and with control over parish schools and property; it remained the Armenian church's constitution until 1917 and was a means of its integration and the preservation of its influence.
nodes.src: Polozhenie (1836); George Bournoutian, A Concise History of the Armenian People (2002).

nodes.label: Molokans and Dukhobors
nodes.full: Russian dissenting Christians, the Molokans ('milk-drinkers') and the Dukhobors ('spirit-wrestlers'), exiled by Nicholas I in 1830s–1840s from central Russia, were settled in Transcaucasia in the Akhalkalaki district and Karabakh as frontier colonists, and in the 1890s the Dukhobor pacifists would be a cause of dispute with the state.

nodes.label: Baratashvili
nodes.full: Nikoloz Baratashvili, a young Georgian poet of the nobility who died at 27, wrote some forty lyrics, among them 'The Steed' (Merani) and 'Meditation on the Banks of the Mtkvari', that gave the national literature a Romantic voice of personal feeling and love of country, and, together with Grigol Orbeliani, mark its turn from tradition.

nodes.label: Abovian and Raffi
nodes.full: Khachatur Abovian (1809–1848), the founder of modern Armenian literature, wrote the novel 'Wounds of Armenia' about the Russo-Persian war in 1841 (printed 1858), in the vernacular of Ararat's plain; Raffi (Hakob Melik-Hakobian, 1835–1888) published his first novels in the 1860s and 1870s, such as 'Jalaleddin' (1878), and the national revival in Armenian poured out in fiction and verse.
nodes.src: Abovian, Verk Hayastani (Wounds of Armenia); Raffi, Jalaleddin; Suny 1993.

nodes.label: Natavan
nodes.full: Khurshidbanu Natavan, daughter of the last khan of Karabakh and the most important woman poet of Azerbaijan, held a literary society, 'Majlis-i-uns', at Shusha and wrote ghazals in Azerbaijani on love and grief; she is the best known of the poets of the Karabakh school of the 1860s.

nodes.label: Theatre of Tbilisi and Baku
nodes.full: Under Vorontsov, Tbilisi's theatre (the opera house of 1851) staged Russian, Italian and then Georgian and Armenian plays; in Baku the first Azerbaijani-language performance took place in 1873 under the direction of Hasan bey Zardabi, and Akhundov's comedies, written in the 1850s, were acted by amateurs.

nodes.label: Tergdaleulebi
nodes.full: The Georgian students who had studied at St Petersburg in the 1850s and 1860s and returned, 'those who drank the water of the Terek' (Tergdaleulebi), among them Ilia Chavchavadze, Akaki Tsereteli, Niko Nikoladze and Giorgi Tsereteli, edited journals and wrote in favour of the Georgian language, the peasants' emancipation and national consciousness, creating the modern Georgian national movement.
nodes.src: Ilia Chavchavadze, Is a Man a Man? (1863); Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Nalbandian
nodes.full: Mikael Nalbandian (1829–1866), a poet, essayist and radical, who was imprisoned in 1862–1866 for contacts with the Russian revolutionary Herzen, wrote 'Freedom' (Azatutyun) and political pamphlets and argued for a secular, popular education; the journals 'Ararat', 'Hyusisapayl' and 'Mshak' (1872) set the course of the Armenian press.

nodes.label: Akhundov and Zardabi
nodes.full: Mirza Fatali Akhundov (1812–1878), a teacher of Persian and Azerbaijani at Tbilisi, wrote six comedies in Azerbaijani in the 1850s attacking superstition, and proposed reform of the Arabic script; Hasan bey Zardabi (1842–1907) founded 'Akinchi' (The Ploughman) in 1875, the first newspaper in Azerbaijani, in Baku.

nodes.label: Brosset
nodes.full: The French orientalist Marie-Félicité Brosset (1802–1880), a member of the Academy of Sciences at St Petersburg, published from 1849 translations of the Georgian chronicles, Armenian historians and Georgian inscriptions, and with Russian officials and scholars made the sources of Caucasian history available in Europe.
nodes.src: Brosset, Histoire de la Géorgie (1849–1858); Collection d'historiens arméniens (1874–1876).

nodes.label: Baku oil boom
nodes.full: The first drilled oil well in the world on an industrial scale was bored at Bibi-Heybat near Baku in 1846; the abolition of the state monopoly in 1872 and the open auction of oil lands led to a boom, in which Ludwig Nobel arrived in 1873 and built a refinery in 1876. Baku's output rose from a few thousand tonnes to hundreds of thousands in the 1870s.

nodes.label: Poti–Tbilisi railway
nodes.full: The first railway of Transcaucasia, from the Black Sea port of Poti to Tbilisi, was opened in stages from 1872 to carry the cargoes of the Black Sea trade, and the line later was extended to Baku in 1883; the railway connected Georgia's farmland to markets and made Tbilisi a commercial centre.

nodes.label: Tbilisi economy
nodes.full: Tbilisi, a free-trade centre in the 1830s with the benefit of its transit trade with Persia and Turkey, grew from some 30,000 to 100,000 people by 1870s; its craftsmen's guilds (amkari) were replaced by factories and merchant houses, many of them Armenian, and its wine, silk and leather were exported.

nodes.label: Steamers and telegraph
nodes.full: The Caucasus and Mercury steamship company, founded in 1858, ran steamers on the Caspian and the Volga, and the telegraph connected Tbilisi with Russia (1850s) and Baku (1860s); with the military road and the Poti railway, these changed communications in the province.

nodes.label: Muhajirism
nodes.full: After the end of the Caucasian War in 1864 the Russian authorities pushed or allowed several hundred thousand Muslim Circassians and Abkhaz to emigrate to the Ottoman empire, and after the rising of 1866 and the war of 1877–1878 a large share of Abkhazia's Muslim population left. Abkhaz historians and some scholars call the expulsions genocide; the Russian state and others call them emigration under war conditions; the numbers are disputed.
nodes.src: Imperial reports; Stephen Shenfield, 'The Circassians: A Forgotten Genocide?' (1999); Walter Richmond, The Circassian Genocide (2013); Suny 1994.

nodes.label: Treaty of Berlin
nodes.full: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which revised the treaty of San Stefano, the Ottomans ceded Kars, Ardahan and Batum to Russia, which organised Kars as an oblast and Batum as a free port, making Russia the neighbour of Erzurum and setting the Caucasian border for forty years.

nodes.label: Cholera and population
nodes.full: Cholera swept the Caucasus in 1830, 1847–1848 and 1865, killing tens of thousands, and plague broke out in the 1830s; in spite of this and the wars the population grew, by roughly a doubling between 1830 and the 1880s, with the Armenian and Georgian numbers growing and the proportion of Muslims falling.

nodes.label: Princesses of Tsinandali
nodes.full: Princess Anna Chavchavadze, her sister Varvara Orbeliani, their families and servants, among them children and the French governess Madame Drancey, were held in Dagestan by Shamil for eight months; Anna's recollections tell of their treatment and the ransom. The Chavchavadze family was among the leaders of Georgian culture.
nodes.src: Anna Chavchavadze's account of the captivity; Gammer 1994.

nodes.label: Natavan
nodes.full: Khurshidbanu Natavan, the khan's daughter, who had lost her family's rule and her children, held a salon and gave money to schools and for the poor of Shusha, and had a spring (the 'Khan gizi bulagi') named after her. She is the best known woman of the Azerbaijani Enlightenment.

nodes.label: Artisan and serf
nodes.full: Tbilisi's artisans of the amkari, among them Armenian and Georgian craftsmen, lived in the old town of Avlabari, Sololaki and Kala, with a rigid hierarchy, and Georgia's serfs, some two-fifths of the rural population, worked the estates and owed labour and dues; the emancipation of the 1860s tried to ease the rural poor but left debts.

nodes.label: Turkmenchay and the Armenian Oblast
nodes.full: By the treaty of Turkmenchay (10 February 1828) Persia ceded Erivan and Nakhchivan to Russia, and the Armenian Oblast was created on 21 March 1828; the Russian conquest of the Caucasus south of the range was complete.
